title: Lunceford's band, Willie Smith and Harry James's baseball
summary: He knew many Lunceford players and singers, and recalls Willie Smith's drinking in the Harry James band and Woody's band beating them at softball.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: And I'll always regret that I never got to meet Dick Wilson. I did get to know Don Byas pretty well. But I never got to know Pha Terrell. I did know Dan Grissom very

well. I got to know the guys in Lunceford's band very well, all of them. Joe Thomas is one of my best friends. And I worked with Willie Smith out in Los Angeles, when he just... before he was getting very sick.

The last time I saw him was when Charlie Barnet brought him into New York with a band he put together, a band here for Basin Street East, and Willie was the only guy he brought with him, you know, to play lead. That was the last time I saw him.

Well, see... The guys that worked with Harry James were working a very dangerous job, because it was the heaviest drinking band, outside of Casa Loma, in the world. And the heaviest drinker of the whole band was the leader. And between that and baseball, hard baseball, you didn't belong in the band. So consequently, Willie just turned into an out-and-out lush. I mean, good Lord, it was terrible. Of course, Lester Young would have drank 'em all out of the room.
And Harry was crazy about baseball.

Oh yeah. Everybody that had a car in that band, he opened up the case in the back -- there's the uniform and the cleats and the bats and the gloves... They weren't any good at it either. We played 'em one time and beat 'em.

Woody. Yeah, we beat 'em. Played the hard softball. That was funny. Boy, they were mad. They didn't think anybody could beat 'em; they were too good. I said, "You ain't too good. You're too busy at the bar."
